learningObjective: Explain the pipeline-parallel bubble and how microbatching reduces it.

canonicalClaims.claim: In pipeline parallelism with P stages and M microbatches, the classical GPipe-style schedule has a bubble fraction of (P-1)/(P + M - 1) of the total time; increasing M reduces the fraction of time spent in the bubble.
conditions: All microbatches have equal per-stage cost.
Forward and backward are pipelined identically (or the schedule accounts for the split).
Communication between stages is overlapped or negligible relative to compute.
nonImplications: Does not imply the bubble ever reaches zero — with a finite M there is always a fill/drain period of P-1 stages.
Does not imply that M can be increased without limit; larger M means more activations to keep alive (or recomputation), raising memory pressure.

sourceMappings.locator: Ch. 6 discussion of pipeline parallelism and utilization

misconceptions.claim: The pipeline bubble is a property of the compiler, not the schedule; a smart compiler can eliminate it entirely for any P and M.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The bubble is inherent to fill/drain of a P-stage pipeline with finite microbatches; better schedules (1F1B, interleaved) can hide but not eliminate it below a fundamental floor.

misconceptions.claim: Increasing the number of microbatches M has no effect on memory usage; only P matters.
misconceptions.whyWrong: In GPipe, all M microbatches keep activations alive until backward; memory scales with M. Recomputation or 1F1B mitigates but does not eliminate this trade-off.

misconceptions.claim: Pipeline parallelism reduces the wall-clock time of a single microbatch's forward+backward compared to running the whole model on one device.
misconceptions.whyWrong: For a single microbatch, pipeline adds inter-stage communication and does not shorten critical-path compute. Pipelining amortizes across many microbatches to raise throughput.
